title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review Standards, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Purpose
This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budget policies, capacity planning guidance, reliability initiative templates, incident review requirements, recommended operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended to standardize how teams measure, react to, and improve service reliability across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope
- Applies to all customer-facing inference and control-plane services owned by the Platform and Serving teams.
- Not intended for short-lived experimental services without production traffic; those teams should adopt these standards when traffic stabilizes.

Key definitions
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): measurable signal (e.g., successful request rate, p95 latency).
- SLO: target or objective expressed over an SLI and a time window (e.g., 99.95% availability over 30 days).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO (the allowed proportion of bad events over the SLO window).
- Burn rate: rate at which the error budget is being consumed relative to expected.

1) SLO and Error Budget Standards
1.1 SLO naming and format
- Use the pattern: <service> / <endpoint-group> / <objective> (e.g., runtime/generation-api/availability-99.95-30d).
- SLOs must specify: SLI definition, target (percentage or latency), measurement window, and owner.

1.2 Required SLOs by service class
- Control plane services (auth, billing, routing): availability SLO = 99.99% monthly (rolling 30d).
- Public inference endpoints (hosted API): availability SLO = 99.95% monthly (rolling 30d); p95 latency SLO = 300ms for small payloads; p95 = 600ms for large payloads (configurable per model family).
- Dedicated/Private management plane: availability SLO = 99.9% monthly.
- Background/worker jobs: job success-rate SLO = 99% per 7-day window and documented runbook.

1.3 Example SLO table
| service | SLI | SLO | window | owner |
|--------|-----|-----:|:-----:|:-----|
| runtime/generation-api | successful responses (2xx) excluding rate-limited requests | 99.95% | 30d | serving-runtime@redwood.com |
| runtime/generation-api | p95 latency (small payloads) | <300ms | 30d | serving-runtime@redwood.com |
| controlplane/auth | successful token exchanges | 99.99% | 30d | eng-platform@redwood.com |

1.4 Measurement and tooling
- SLIs must be implemented as production queries with a single authoritative source (Prometheus + Thanos for metrics; ClickHouse for production request logs where applicable).
- Provide the query used to calculate each SLI in the SLO configuration page (example PromQL below).
Example PromQL (availability):
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="runtime",status=~"2.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="runtime"}[30d]))
Example p95 (histogram):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="runtime"}[30d])) by (le))

1.5 Error budget policy and actions
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. Use rolling window matching the SLO.
- Thresholds and automated responses:
  - Informational: burn > 20% in last 7 days -> notify owners and product manager; schedule investigation within 5 business days.
  - Operational intervention: burn > 50% in last 7 days OR > 25% in last 24 hours -> require conference call, pause risky releases, and execute mitigation runbook.
  - All-hands response: burn > 90% in last 24 hours -> invoke incident response, escalate to SRE manager and VP Eng, consider immediate rollback/traffic-shift.
- Releases: if error budget is >50% consumed in the current SLO window, no non-critical production releases (including model rollouts or quantization changes) until the budget is back in healthy range or a mitigation plan is approved.

2) Capacity planning
2.1 Objectives
- Ensure capacity to meet SLOs with 99.9% confidence for expected traffic patterns and planned growth for the next quarter.
- Reduce risk of capacity-driven incidents by maintaining clear headroom and automated scaling where possible.

2.2 Capacity model and inputs
- Inputs: baseline qps by route, per-request token distribution, average sequence length, model memory/KV requirements, batching efficiency, per-GPU throughput, maintenance windows, and growth forecast.
- Model output: required GPU count by class (A100, H100, etc.), reserved headroom percentage, and autoscaler settings.

2.3 Standard headroom targets (guideline)
- Hosted public endpoints: reserve 30% headroom on peak-of-day capacity for the default cluster; enable burst pool for 2x baseline for short durations.
- Dedicated clusters: reserve 15% headroom; contract commitments should reflect steady-state throughput plus 15% buffer.
- Private/on-prem: conservative default headroom 40% until validated by 2 quarters of telemetry.

2.4 Forecasting cadence and owners
- Quarterly capacity review run by eng-sre and eng-platform with inputs from product and sales for Dedicated contracts. Deliverables: capacity plan spreadsheet, scaling playbook, and a prioritized list of capacity purchase/scale tasks.

2.5 Capacity incident runbook (summary)
1. Detect: alert when utilization > 90% sustained for 10 minutes or P95 latency SLO breach coincident with high utilization.
2. Triage: identify hot routes, top 5 callers, and recent deploys.
3. Mitigate: increase autoscaler limits, move non-critical workloads to burst pool, throttle or degrade non-essential features (e.g., reduce candidate count), and contact sales for high-impact customers.
4. Postmortem: create incident in the incident tracker and link telemetry; include capacity model updates and purchase actions.

3) Reliability initiatives and continuous improvement
3.1 Initiative structure
- All reliability initiatives must have: objective, measurable success criteria (KPIs), owner, timeline, and rollback criteria. Use the Reliability Initiative template in product-docs/roadmap.

3.2 Example initiatives (Q1-Q2 playbook)
- Initiative: Prefix caching for cold model runs -> KPI: reduce p95 tokens served cost by 12%; owner: serving-runtime; target: complete canary by end of Q1.
- Initiative: Autoscaler tuning to reduce overprovisioning -> KPI: lower reserved GPU hours by 18% across hosted clusters; owner: eng-sre; target: Q2.

3.3 Post-initiative evaluation
- After deployment, evaluate impact against pre-defined KPIs using a 30/60/90 day window. If regressions occur, open a regression triage and hold further rollouts.

4) Incident review and postmortem standards
4.1 Required timeline
- Incident severity classification must be set within 2 hours of detection.
- Draft postmortem within 72 hours; final postmortem published within 10 business days.

4.2 Postmortem template (mandatory sections)
- Summary: what happened in one paragraph.
- Impact: services affected, customers impacted, duration, and SLO implications.
- Timeline: succinct timeline with timestamps.
- Root cause analysis: factual causes (no blame).
- Contributing factors: system and process issues.
- Corrective actions: short-term and long-term actions with owners and due dates.
- Follow-up: link to related change requests, capacity plan updates, and verification steps.

4.3 Review process
- Every postmortem must be reviewed by at least one cross-team reviewer (not from the incident response team) and the SRE manager. Reviews must verify that corrective actions have owners and dates.
- High-severity incidents require an all-hands incident review meeting within 5 business days.

5) Operational tooling and dashboards
5.1 Canonical dashboards (minimum set)
- Service Health Overview: SLO burn rate, availability, and top errors (per service).
- Latency Distribution: p50/p95/p99 by route and model family.
- Capacity & Utilization: GPU utilization by pool, queue lengths, and batch sizes.
- Top customers by QPS and token consumption.
- Error budget dashboard: per-service burn and projected exhaustion date.

5.2 Alerts and thresholding guidance
- Alert on symptoms, not only SLO breaches. Examples: 5xx rate spike > 0.5% of requests for 5 minutes; sustained p95 increase > 2x baseline for 10 minutes; GPU utilization > 92% for 10 minutes.
- Use multi-window alerting: short-term (5-15m) for operational triage, medium-term (1-3h) for escalation, long-term (24h) for capacity planning.
- Alert routing: critical alerts -> primary on-call for owning service, paging escalation to SRE rotation; informational -> slack channel with owner mention.

5.3 Tooling integrations
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos, aggregated into Grafana dashboards.
- Traces: OpenTelemetry -> Jaeger/Tempo.
- Logs: structured logs into ClickHouse for ad-hoc queries and into a long-term ELK/ClickHouse cluster.
- Incident management: PagerDuty for paging; linear/jira for postmortems and follow-ups.

6) Runbooks (canonical examples)
6.1 High 5xx rate (runtime/generation-api)
- Trigger: 5xx rate > 0.5% sustained for 5 minutes or error budget intervention threshold.
- Owner: runtime on-call -> serving-runtime rotation.
- Steps:
  1. Confirm: query last 15 minutes for error codes, top endpoints, and top callers. Example ClickHouse query: SELECT status, count() FROM requests WHERE service='generation-api' AND timestamp > now()-15*60 GROUP BY status ORDER BY count DESC;
  2. Check recent deploys: list last 3 deploys and roll out times.
  3. If errors concentrated on recent deploy: rollback the deploy (CLI command: cd infra && ./deploy rollback --service generation-api --to-tag <previous>).
  4. If errors concentrated by route or caller: apply temporary route throttles or rate-limits via the traffic-control service (CLI example: trafficctl throttle --route /v1/generate --rate 20rps).
  5. If infrastructure-related (GPU OOM, disk pressure): move traffic to burst pool and scale up extra nodes.
  6. Open incident, notify stakeholders, and create postmortem using template.

6.2 High P95 latency (runtime/generation-api)
- Trigger: p95 latency breach for 15 minutes or latency contributes to SLO burn > 25% in 24h.
- Steps:
  1. Identify slow routes and model families.
  2. Check batch sizes and queue lengths; temporarily reduce max batch size to lower tail latency.
  3. If model memory or KV cache pressure is detected, restart affected workers in a staggered fashion.
  4. If due to burst traffic, engage autoscaler to increase target replicas and enable burst pool.
  5. If caused by a recent model change, revert model variant or disable quantization profile until stable.

6.3 Capacity saturation runbook
- Trigger: GPU pool utilization > 92% for 10 minutes or queued requests > 1000.
- Steps:
  1. Identify offending workloads and top requesters.
  2. Move low-priority customers to best-effort pool.
  3. Increase autoscaler max and start warm nodes (command: infractl scale --pool runtime-default --count +4).
  4. If additional capacity cannot be provisioned within 30 minutes, follow customer communication playbook and consider temporary traffic shaping.

7) Ownership, reviews, and cadence
- SLO owners must maintain SLO config pages with queries and owners. Changes to SLOs must be approved in writing by the SRE manager and product owner.
- Monthly SLO review: each team reviews SLO state and error budget burn with SRE during a 30-minute slot.
- Quarterly reliability retro: present initiative outcomes and capacity forecasts to Eng leadership.

Appendix A - Sample SLO entry (copy into service SLO page)
- Title: runtime/generation-api/availability-99.95-30d
- SLI: ratio of 2xx responses to total non-rate-limited requests (PromQL provided).
- Target: 99.95%
- Window: 30d (rolling)
- Owner: serving-runtime@redwood.com
- Measurement: Prometheus metric http_requests_total with labels {service="generation-api", status=~"2.."}
- Error budget policy: see section 1.5.
